notes:
I've drafted notes for every verse, but the research has gaps you should know about first:

- **No Catholic, Orthodox or debated popular teaching sources.** My searches ran out before I could look at newadvent.org (Augustine), catholic.com, oca.org or any prosperity or word-of-faith material, so those sections are missing.
- **No real split between Protestant traditions.** The Reformed, Baptist and other teachers I read differ in emphasis, not in what the verses mean. The genuine disagreements I found are between interpreters in general, mainly on how to translate vv. 3, 5, 13–14 and on what "awake" means in v. 15.
- **Some pages were read only in part.** Enduring Word was cut off partway through vv. 10–14, and I only saw extracts of Gill, Calvin, Spurgeon and Matthew Henry.

---

## Psalm 17: Verse-by-verse notes

**Title / overall**
- Guzik says the psalm can't be tied to one moment in David's life. He calls it marked by trust in God, lack of confidence in self and a "glorious heavenly hope." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-17/
- Ellicott thinks Psalms 16 and 17 were probably written by the same person and points to parallels between them. He says the speaker could also stand for the righteous part of Israel suffering under the ungodly, and then the authorship question matters less. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/17.htm
- Matthew Henry's outline: David appeals to God about his integrity (vv. 1–4), asks to be kept in it and protected (vv. 5–8, 13), describes his enemies (vv. 9–12, 14), and takes comfort in future happiness (v. 15). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_017.cfm

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading:** Calvin says David, sure of his integrity, asks God to judge between him and his enemies. Calvin adds that a good conscience isn't enough by itself, so David prays as well. He says "cry" and "prayer" mean the same thing; saying it twice shows how earnest David is. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/17.htm
- Spurgeon notes that David asks to be heard three times in this one verse, because he fears his voice will be drowned out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/17-1.htm
- Barnes: this was prayer spoken aloud, not just a silent wish. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-17.html
- Guzik's caution: both sides in a quarrel can feel sure they are right, so readers shouldn't automatically claim David's words for their own cause. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-17/
- Matthew Henry: "lips free of deceit" means David meant what he said, and insincere prayers are fruitless. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_017.cfm
- **Other readings:** Ellicott says some ancient versions read "Hear, Lord of righteousness," but the familiar sense is correct. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/17.htm
- Spurgeon mentions Jerome's rendering, "Hear the just One," taken to mean the Messiah. Spurgeon thinks it works as a plea in prayer whether or not it is the right translation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/17-1.htm

**v. 2**
- Ellicott: David asks for his case to be tried in God's court, where he expects to win because he is innocent and God is just. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/17.htm
- Guzik: David refused to take matters into his own hands, as he did when he spared Saul. He wanted his vindication to be God's work, not his own. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-17/
- Pulpit: like Job, David has no doubt what the verdict will be. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/17.htm

**v. 3**
- **Traditional reading:** Pulpit says "found no evil" doesn't mean David was sinless. It means God found no serious flaw: David was sincere, not a hypocrite. Night is when God's searching thoughts are hardest to escape. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/17.htm
- Ellicott: night is the time of calm reflection and self-examination. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/17.htm
- Guzik: letting God test your heart means being willing to be told you are wrong. Open, unconfessed sin blocks prayer (quoting Boice). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-17/
- **Gill (Baptist), a Christ-centred reading:** "my mouth will not sin" means not complaining against God or insulting accusers. Gill links this to Christ, who did not hit back when insulted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-17.html
- **Translation debate:** Ellicott says the word behind "I have resolved" is hard. He prefers to read it as a noun ("evil plans") belonging to the line before: God finds no malice in him, and none passes his lips. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/17.htm

**v. 4**
- Barnes: David avoided evil not by his own strength but through God's commands and promises. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/17-4.htm
- On the same page, a commentator ties this to David sparing Saul's life when he could have taken it, out of obedience to God's word. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/17-4.htm
- Spurgeon: without God's grace using God's word to protect us, we would soon copy the worst of men. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps017.cfm
- Coffman, citing Ash: since God's revelation is itself grace, David isn't pleading his own merit alone. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-17.html
- Maclaren notes the contrast between David's closed mouth and God's lips: only someone who silences much of what rises in his heart can hear God speak. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/17.htm

**v. 5**
- **Prayer or statement?** Older versions (KJV, NKJV) read this as a prayer, "Uphold my steps." Guzik takes it that way: David wants to be kept only on God's paths. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-17/
- Ellicott says it is a statement, not a prayer, because David is still declaring his innocence (this is how the BSB reads it). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/17.htm
- Pulpit agrees that most recent critics read it as a statement. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/17.htm

**v. 6**
- Guzik: David is calmly confident even though the crisis isn't over. Boice says the psalm models prayer that argues its case, not to persuade God but to sharpen what we ask. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-17/
- Pulpit: having shown his sincerity in vv. 3–5, David goes back to his request. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/17.htm

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: the verb literally means "set apart." It is used of God's special care for Israel and so carries a sense of wonder. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/17.htm
- Spurgeon: it is the same word as Psalm 4:3, as if David asks God to set apart His choicest mercies for him now. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps017.cfm
- Utley: the word for love here (*hesed*) means God's loyal, steadfast covenant love. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-17
- Maclaren: the prayer sounds arrogant but is really humble, since the wonder is that God would show such love to someone like him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/17.htm
- Guzik: believers shouldn't settle for "moderate" expectations of God's love. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-17/
- Pulpit: it is unclear whether "by Your right hand" goes with God saving or with those who rise up against Him. Most follow the KJV. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/17.htm

**v. 8**
- Ellicott: "apple of the eye" is literally the "little man, daughter of the eye," meaning the tiny reflection you see in someone's pupil. The wings image usually means an eagle or vulture and comes from Deuteronomy 32:10–11. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/17.htm
- Benson: God shelters His people from visible and invisible enemies, as a hen shelters her chicks. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/17-8.htm
- Guzik: the pupil stands for something precious and easily hurt. The same image appears in Deuteronomy 32:10, Proverbs 7:2 and Zechariah 2:8, and Jesus used the wings picture in Matthew 23:37. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-17/

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: "mortal enemies" is literally enemies "against the life." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/17.htm
- Matthew Henry: these were enemies of David's soul, trying to drive him to serve other gods (1 Samuel 26:19). The worst enemies are those who are enemies to our souls. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_017.cfm
- Pulpit links this to Saul hunting David in the hills. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/17.htm

**v. 10**
- Pulpit: "closed their callous hearts" is literally "enclosed in their own fat." Self-indulgence has hardened and dulled them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/17.htm
- Horne (quoted by Guzik): pride is the child of plenty. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-17/
- Ellicott: "fat" is a picture of the conceit that prosperity breeds. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/17.htm

**v. 11**
- Gill: the enemies were always at their heels, as when Saul chased David to Keilah and Maon. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-17.html
- Ellicott calls the Hebrew text confused. He mentions a proposed reading: "they have set their eyes to shed our blood on the earth." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/17.htm
- Calvin: fixing their eyes means putting all their effort into overthrowing him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/17.htm

**v. 12**
- Pulpit: like a young lion at full strength, crouching just before it springs. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/17.htm

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: "confront them" means going out to meet the enemy as a champion. The KJV's "the wicked, which is thy sword" is wrong; it should read "with Your sword." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/17.htm
- Calvin: God's sword is set against all human help. Without God's own action David has no hope. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/17.htm
- Pulpit: justice means both rescuing the godly and punishing the ungodly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/17.htm

**v. 14**
- Pulpit: "men of the world" are people whose hopes stop at this life, the "children of this world" of Luke 16:8. The verse points to the worldly prosperity of the wicked, which their children seldom keep. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/17.htm
- **Translation note:** in the KJV the full bellies belong to the wicked. The BSB applies the blessing to God's "treasured ones." Ellicott notes that the word for God's stored treasure is used in both good and bad senses elsewhere. He contrasts "their portion in this life" with Psalm 16:5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/17.htm

**v. 15 (the most debated verse)**
- **Waking after death:** Pulpit says David has already called death a sleep (Psalm 13:3), so "awake" must mean waking from death. The word for "likeness" is the one used of God's glory shown to Moses (Numbers 12:8). Pulpit sees a kind of beatific vision here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/psalms/17.htm
- Barnes: only a future world could give the lasting comfort David needed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bnb/psalms-17.html
- Guzik: the hope starts now but is completed in eternity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-17/
- **Waking from ordinary sleep:** Ellicott lists other views (relief after trouble, recovery from illness, grace dawning). He himself leans to waking after a night's sleep, because v. 3 mentions the night. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/psalms/17.htm
- **In between:** Maclaren thinks the psalmist probably had no clear idea of a future life, but was sure of one because fellowship with God felt like it must be immortal. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/17.htm
- **Two emphases on "in righteousness":**
  - Matthew Henry reads it as being clothed in Christ's righteousness and seeing God's likeness in His word and in our renewed lives. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_017.cfm
  - Calvin (Reformed) says David's highest happiness is knowing God is reconciled to him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/psalms/17.htm
- **Spurgeon's collection:** the sincere Christian keeps moving forward and is never at journey's end until heaven. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps017.cfm
